value.text:
h01.

The S3 presign runner (`s3presign.Runner`, defined in `server/runner/s3presign/runner.go`) is what keeps S3-backed attachment links fresh. It re-presigns GET URLs for every attachment whose storage type is S3 and writes the new URL back into the attachment's `Reference` field, stamping `LastPresignedTime` in the payload. It walks attachments in batches of 100 and skips any whose presigned URL is still valid for at least the next 4 days (URLs are issued with a 5-day expiration), so each pass only refreshes what's close to going stale.

**s3presign.Runner (`server/runner/s3presign/runner.go`) — once immediately at startup, then every 12 hours on a ticker (`runnerInterval = time.Hour * 12`, line 27) — wired in `server/server.go:162-171`**

The wiring lives in `Server.startBackgroundRunners`, called from `Server.Start` at `server/server.go:129`:

```161:171:server/server.go
	// Create and start S3 presign runner
	s3presignRunner := s3presign.NewRunner(s.Store)
	s3presignRunner.RunOnce(ctx)

	// Start continuous S3 presign runner
	s.backgroundRunnerWG.Add(1)
	go func() {
		defer s.backgroundRunnerWG.Done()
		s3presignRunner.Run(s3Context)
		slog.Info("s3presign runner stopped")
	}()
```

Note the runner is constructed at `server/server.go:162`, does a synchronous first pass via `RunOnce` at line 163, and the periodic loop starts in the goroutine at line 169 using a dedicated cancellable context (`s3Context`, created at line 156) whose cancel function is registered for shutdown at line 159.

value.text:
h02.

**`webhook.Post` — `internal/webhook/webhook.go:120` (the function that builds and sends the HTTP POST; line 152 is the actual `safeClient.Do(req)` call); protection is a dial-time SSRF guard, `safeDialContext` + `isReservedIP` — `internal/webhook/webhook.go:59` and `internal/webhook/validate.go:44`, with a store-time check via `webhook.ValidateURL` — `internal/webhook/validate.go:62`**

How it fits together:

**Delivery.** Memo create/update/delete and comment-created events call `webhook.PostAsync` from `server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go:43` and `:71`. `PostAsync` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:184`) only enqueues onto a buffered channel of 128, dropping with a warning when full. Four worker goroutines started in `init()` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:42-55`) drain that queue and call `Post`, so the real outbound request always executes on a background worker, never on the request goroutine. `Post` marshals the payload, optionally adds Standard Webhooks HMAC-SHA256 headers (`webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, `webhook-signature`), and issues the request through `safeClient`.

**Protection.** The primary defense is at the transport layer rather than the URL layer. `safeClient` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:32-37`) is built with a `http.Transport` whose `DialContext` is `safeDialContext`. That function splits the host/port, resolves the hostname itself via `net.DefaultResolver.LookupHost`, and refuses to dial if any resolved address is in a reserved range. Because the check happens at dial time on the addresses actually being connected to, it also defeats DNS rebinding, where a hostname passes validation at save time and later resolves to something internal.

The reserved ranges are declared in `internal/webhook/validate.go:14-23` and cover IPv4 loopback, all three RFC-1918 private blocks, link-local `169.254.0.0/16` (which includes the cloud instance metadata endpoint at `169.254.169.254`), plus the IPv6 equivalents (`::1/128`, `fc00::/7`, `fe80::/10`). They're parsed once in an `init()` at line 28, which panics on a malformed CIDR.

There's also a secondary check at configuration time: `webhook.ValidateURL` is called before webhooks are persisted, from `server/router/api/v1/user_service_webhooks.go:74`, `:161`, and `:182`. It requires an absolute `http`/`https` URL and rejects hostnames resolving into reserved ranges, giving the user an `InvalidArgument` error up front instead of a silent delivery failure later.

Both layers share the `isReservedIP` helper (`internal/webhook/validate.go:44`), which has a global escape hatch: the exported `AllowPrivateIPs` flag disables the SSRF protection entirely when true. It's wired to the `allow-private-webhooks` config option in `cmd/memos/main.go:49`, intended for self-hosted setups whose webhook targets legitimately live on the local network.

value.text:
h03.

**`internal/idp` (`internal/idp/idp.go`); `internal/idp/oauth2` (`internal/idp/oauth2/oauth2.go`)**

The abstraction in `internal/idp` is deliberately thin: `idp.go` is a nine-line file that defines only the `IdentityProviderUserInfo` struct with `Identifier`, `DisplayName`, `Email`, and `AvatarURL`. There is no Go interface declaring `ExchangeToken`/`UserInfo` methods, so the shared contract is the normalized user-info type that every provider must produce, not a polymorphic interface.

OAuth2 is the only concrete protocol that ships. `internal/idp/oauth2/oauth2.go` defines an `IdentityProvider` wrapping a `storepb.OAuth2Config`, with `NewIdentityProvider` validating that client ID, client secret, token URL, user-info URL, and the identifier field mapping are all non-empty (lines 27-43). `ExchangeToken` (line 47) performs the authorization-code exchange via `golang.org/x/oauth2` and supports PKCE by passing `code_verifier` when supplied. `UserInfo` (line 83) calls the user-info endpoint with a 10-second timeout and a bearer token, then maps arbitrary JSON claims onto `idp.IdentityProviderUserInfo` using the configured `FieldMapping`, failing if the identifier claim is missing and defaulting display name to the identifier.

The single-implementation design shows up in the schema and the caller too. `proto/store/idp.proto` declares `IdentityProvider.Type` with only `TYPE_UNSPECIFIED` and `OAUTH2` (lines 11-14), and `IdentityProviderConfig` is a `oneof` with just `oauth2_config`. The consumer, `resolveSSOIdentity` in `server/router/api/v1/auth_service_sso.go`, dispatches with a plain `if identityProvider.Type == storepb.IdentityProvider_OAUTH2` at line 120 and constructs `oauth2.NewIdentityProvider` directly rather than resolving through a registry — the only two files importing `internal/idp` are the oauth2 package itself and this SSO handler.

```

Searching all Go files for imports of `github.com/usememos/memos/store/db/...` returns only five import lines: `store/db/db.go:8-10` (the factory importing all three drivers), and `store/demo_seed_test.go:13` plus `store/deployment_config_test.go:19`, which import `store/db/sqlite` — not MySQL. **Handlers: `CreateMemo`, `UpdateMemo`, `DeleteMemo`, `CreateMemoComment`, `SetMemoAttachments`, `SetMemoRelations`; convergence function: `webhook.Post` — `internal/webhook/webhook.go:120` (the actual send is `safeClient.Do(req)` at line 152)**

The user-configured URL comes from each user's stored webhook records (`hook.Url`, read via `s.Store.GetUserWebhooks`), so any handler that reaches a dispatch helper can cause an outbound POST to an address the user chose.

The six handlers, all in `server/router/api/v1`:

| Handler | Path | How it reaches the webhook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CreateMemo` | `memo_service.go:70` | `DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook` at line 157 |
| `UpdateMemo` | `memo_service.go:401` | `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` at line 513 |
| `DeleteMemo` | `memo_service.go:518` | `DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook` at line 562 |
| `CreateMemoComment` | `memo_service_comments.go:20` | `DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook` at line 119 |
| `SetMemoAttachments` | `memo_attachment_service.go:16` | `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` at line 48 |
| `SetMemoRelations` | `memo_relation_service.go:16` | `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` at line 48 |

The last three of those four "updated" paths are worth calling out because the webhook is not obvious from the handler name: `SetMemoAttachments` and `SetMemoRelations` both call the shared helper `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` (`memo_update_helpers.go:66`), which fires `DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook` before broadcasting the SSE event. So changing a memo's attachment list or relations emits a `memos.memo.updated` webhook just as `UpdateMemo` does.

The funnel below the handlers is narrow. The four `Dispatch*Webhook` methods in `server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go` all resolve the owner's webhooks and call `webhook.PostAsync` (lines 43 and 71). `PostAsync` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:184`) only enqueues onto a 128-slot buffered channel; four worker goroutines started in `init()` (lines 42-55) drain it and every one of them calls `Post`. `Post` is therefore the single chokepoint where the request is built, optionally HMAC-signed, and sent — which is also why the SSRF guard is installed there, on the shared `safeClient`'s dialer rather than at each call site.

The browser hits `GET /file/users/{username}/avatar` — a plain HTTP route on the Echo server, not the gRPC-Gateway API. That URL is what the API hands out: `convertUserFromStore` rewrites a base64 avatar into `/file/{user.Name}/avatar` (`server/router/api/v1/user_service_converters.go:36`) so the image bytes don't bloat every user payload.

Hops from request to stored data:

`RegisterRoutes` (route `GET /file/users/:identifier/avatar`) — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go:124`
`FileServerService.serveUserAvatar` — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go:168`
`FileServerService.getCurrentUser` → `auth.Authenticator.AuthenticateToUser` (only when `Profile.AllowAnonymous()` is false) — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go:708`
`FileServerService.getUserByUsername` — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go:715`
`Store.GetUser` (user cache checked only for lookups by ID, so a username lookup always falls through) — `store/user.go:148`
`Store.ListUsers` — `store/user.go:136`
`store.Driver.ListUsers` (interface) — `store/driver.go:47`
`DB.ListUsers` (`SELECT ... avatar_url ... FROM user WHERE username = ?`) — `store/db/sqlite/user.go:88` (SQL at line 150-165, execution at line 173; parallel implementations in `store/db/mysql/user.go` and `store/db/postgres/user.go`)

Back in the handler, the stored value is not a file path or blob reference — `user.AvatarURL` holds a data URI, which `parseDataURI` (`server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go:737`) splits into MIME type and decoded bytes with a regex. The type is checked against `avatarAllowedTypes` (`fileserver.go:75`), then security headers and `Cache-Control` are set and the bytes go out via `c.Blob` (line 209).

Two access-control details worth noting: the `identifier` path segment is matched against `username` only, and anonymous requests are rejected with 401 when the instance has no `InstanceURL` configured (lines 173-181), so on a private instance another user's avatar requires a valid session, access token, or PAT.

**Count: 8 method declarations named `Close` (6 in production code, 2 in test files). Invoked from non-test server code: `Store.Close`, `SSEHub.Close`, `cache.Cache.Close`, and the three per-driver `DB.Close` implementations — everything except the two test-context types.**

| Declarer | Path | Invoked by non-test code? | Caller |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `*Store` | `store/store.go:72` | yes | `Server.Shutdown` — `server/server.go:146` |
| `*SSEHub` | `server/router/api/v1/sse_hub.go:99` | yes | `Server.closeLongLivedConnections` — `server/server.go:206` |
| `*cache.Cache` | `store/cache/cache.go:187` | yes | `Store.Close` — `store/store.go:74`, `:75`, `:76` |
| `*DB` (sqlite) | `store/db/sqlite/sqlite.go:67` | yes, via interface | `Store.Close` → `s.driver.Close()` — `store/store.go:78` |
| `*DB` (mysql) | `store/db/mysql/mysql.go:47` | yes, via interface | same — `store/store.go:78` |
| `*DB` (postgres) | `store/db/postgres/postgres.go:46` | yes, via interface | same — `store/store.go:78` |
| `*MemoFilterTestContext` | `store/test/filter_helpers_test.go:200` | no | test-only |
| `*AttachmentFilterTestContext` | `store/test/filter_helpers_test.go:282` | no | test-only |

The whole thing is one shutdown chain rooted at a single production entry point. `Server.Shutdown` calls `s.sseHub.Close()` at `server/server.go:206` to drop long-lived SSE connections (which `http.Server.Shutdown` would otherwise wait on forever), then `s.Store.Close()` at line 146. `Store.Close` stops the three cache cleanup goroutines — `instanceSettingCache`, `userCache`, `userSettingCache`, all typed `*cache.Cache` per `store/store.go:27-29`, so those are direct calls rather than interface dispatch — and finally returns `s.driver.Close()`.

That last call is the only path to the three `DB.Close` methods, and it goes through the `Close() error` method in the `Driver` interface at `store/driver.go:12`. Which concrete one runs depends on `NewDBDriver`'s switch, so exactly one of the three executes per process, but all three are production-reachable. Each simply delegates to `d.db.Close()` on the underlying `*sql.DB`.

Two things I excluded deliberately: `Close()` appearing in the `Driver` interface (`store/driver.go:12`) and the `cache` interface (`store/cache/cache.go:31`) are method specifications, not declarations with bodies. And `store/test/store.go`/`server/router/api/v1/test/test_helper.go:66` do call `Store.Close`, but those are test-support helpers rather than server code, so `Store.Close`'s production caller remains `Server.Shutdown`.

`store.User` is defined at `store/user.go:29` and `store.Memo` at `store/memo.go:35`. Counting distinct directories outside the `store/` tree that reference each type:

`store.User` — `server/auth`, `server/notification`, `server/router/api/v1`, `server/router/api/v1/test`, `server/router/fileserver`, `server/router/frontend` (test file only), `server/router/rss`. Roughly 99 references across those files.

`store.Memo` — `server/notification`, `server/router/api/v1`, `server/router/api/v1/test`, `server/router/frontend` (test file only), `server/router/rss`, `server/runner/memopayload`. Roughly 73 references.

Third place is `store.Attachment` (`store/attachment.go`) at 4 packages — `server/router/api/v1`, `server/router/api/v1/test`, `server/router/fileserver`, `server/router/rss` — then `store.MemoShare`, `store.MemoRelation`, and `store.Inbox` at 3 each, and `store.Reaction` and `store.UserIdentity` at 2 (API layer plus its test package only).

The reason `User` edges out `Memo` is authentication: `server/auth` resolves tokens and sessions to a `*store.User` and doesn't deal in memos at all, and `server/router/fileserver` needs `store.User` both for avatar lookups and for viewer permission checks while touching `store.Attachment` rather than `store.Memo` directly. `Memo` picks up one package `User` lacks, `server/runner/memopayload`, which rebuilds memo payloads.

Method note: I matched `\bstore\.User\b`-style references in all `.go` files, excluding the `store/` tree itself and `web/`, then reduced file paths to their directories. I ignored the `proto/gen/store` hits that showed up for `UserSetting`, `InstanceSetting`, and `IdentityProvider`, since those are generated protobuf types in a package coincidentally named `store` rather than references to the data-layer entities. I also excluded the query-parameter structs (`FindUser`, `UpdateMemo`, `DeleteAttachment`, and similar), which are not persistent entity types; those are more widely referenced still, but they're request descriptors rather than entities.

**Implementation: the unexported `*markdown.service` (goldmark-backed) — `internal/markdown/markdown.go:58`, the only type satisfying the interface. Construction: `markdown.NewService` (`internal/markdown/markdown.go:85`), called exactly once in production at `server/router/api/v1/v1.go:48` inside `NewAPIV1Service`. Holders: `APIV1Service.MarkdownService` (`server/router/api/v1/v1.go:35`), `RSSService.MarkdownService` (`server/router/rss/rss.go:45`), and `memopayload.Runner.MarkdownService` (`server/runner/memopayload/runner.go:16`), plus the interface passed as a parameter to `memopayload.RebuildMemoPayload` (`server/runner/memopayload/runner.go:74`).**

The interface is `markdown.Service` at `internal/markdown/markdown.go:31`, with eight methods covering extraction (`ExtractAll`, `ExtractTags`, `ExtractProperties`), rendering (`RenderMarkdown`, `RenderHTML`), and utilities (`GenerateSnippet`, `ValidateContent`, `RenameTag`). There is exactly one implementation: the unexported `service` struct wrapping a single `goldmark.Markdown` value. I confirmed uniqueness by searching for any other declaration of the distinctive `ExtractAll(content []byte)` signature — the only hits are the interface method at line 33 and `(*service).ExtractAll` at line 356. No mocks or fakes implement it anywhere, including tests.

Construction is centralized. `NewAPIV1Service` builds the single runtime instance with both custom extensions enabled:

```47:56:server/router/api/v1/v1.go
func NewAPIV1Service(secret string, profile *profile.Profile, store *store.Store) *APIV1Service {
	markdownService := markdown.NewService(
		markdown.WithTagExtension(),
		markdown.WithMentionExtension(),
	)
	return &APIV1Service{
		Secret:                   secret,
		Profile:                  profile,
		Store:                    store,
		MarkdownService:          markdownService,
```

`NewService` composes goldmark with GFM plus the optional `TagExtension` and `MentionExtension` and enables auto heading IDs (lines 91-108), returning `Service` rather than the concrete type.

That one instance is then shared rather than duplicated: `server/server.go:85` passes `apiV1Service.MarkdownService` into `rss.NewRSSService`, so the RSS feed renderer (`RenderHTML` at `server/router/rss/rss.go:339`) uses the same goldmark configuration as the API. 	memo.Payload.Tags = data.Tags
	memo.Payload.Property = data.Property
	return nil
```

Note it overwrites only `Tags` and `Property`, leaving `Payload.Location` intact — which matters because `CreateMemo` sets `create.Payload.Location` from the request immediately *after* the rebuild (`memo_service.go:111-113`), so user-supplied location survives while derived fields are always recomputed from content.

The actual mechanism: `store/cache/cache.go` defines a `Cache` type described as "a thread-safe in-memory cache with TTL and memory management" (line 66), backed by a `sync.Map` plus an atomic item counter. `cache.New` (line 76) starts a background `cleanupLoop` goroutine; there is no dialing, no address, and no serialization, since values are stored as `any` and retrieved with type assertions.

Three separate cache instances are created in `store.New`, all sharing one config literal:

		DefaultTTL:      10 * time.Minute,
		CleanupInterval: 5 * time.Minute,
		MaxItems:        1000,
		OnEviction:      nil,
	}

		driver:               driver,

Note the same 10-minute default is duplicated in `cache.DefaultConfig()` at `store/cache/cache.go:57-64`, but `store.New` builds its own literal rather than calling it.

Two caveats about the TTL that matter in practice. Entries can be dropped before 10 minutes elapse: `MaxItems: 1000` triggers `cleanupOldest()` on insert whenever the count exceeds the cap (`cache.go:117-119`), and the cleanup goroutine sweeps expired entries every 5 minutes, so a logically expired entry may linger until the next sweep unless read. Also, the user cache is only consulted on lookups by ID — `Store.GetUser` checks it only when `find.ID != nil` (`store/user.go:149-156`) — so lookups by username always hit the database.

Because the cache is per-process, a multi-replica deployment gets independent caches with no shared invalidation, which is the practical difference from the Redis setup the question assumed.

**Premise correction: there is no per-user API rate-limiting middleware in this repository. No rate limiter is registered anywhere, and none exists to configure — so there are no request limits to report.**

Evidence for the absence:

A case-insensitive search across all Go files and `go.mod` for `ratelimit`, `rate_limit`, `rate limit`, `throttl`, `golang.org/x/time/rate`, and Echo's `middleware.RateLimiter` returns exactly one hit, and it is an aspirational comment in package documentation rather than code: `internal/email/doc.go:86` lists "Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse" as a suggestion. `golang.org/x/time/rate` is not a dependency.

The full set of middleware registered on the Echo server is four entries: `middleware.Recover()` and `newCORSMiddleware(profile)` at `server/server.go:51-52`, plus static-file serving and an SPA fallback in the frontend router at `server/router/frontend/frontend.go:54` and `:59`. The Connect/gRPC stack has four interceptors — metadata, logging, recovery, and auth (`server/router/api/v1/v1.go:133-137`) — none of which counts or limits requests.

What does exist, and is easy to mistake for rate limiting:

Request **size** caps rather than request **rate** caps: `maxAPIRequestBytes = 256 << 20` (256 MiB) is applied via `http.MaxBytesHandler` on the gateway and Connect handlers and as `connect.WithReadMaxBytes` (`server/router/api/v1/v1.go:20`, `:126`, `:141`, `:144`).

Concurrency semaphores, which bound simultaneous work process-wide rather than per user: three concurrent thumbnail generations and two concurrent image-processing operations in the API service (`server/router/api/v1/v1.go:59-60`), and `maxConcurrentThumbnails = 3` in the file server (`server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go:46`, acquired at line 448). These make callers wait rather than rejecting them, and they are shared across all users.

A bounded webhook dispatch queue of 128 that drops events when full (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:39`) — backpressure on outbound deliveries, not inbound requests.

A per-memo content length limit enforced in `CreateMemo` and `UpdateMemo` via `getContentLengthLimit` (`server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go:101-107` and `:439-445`).

So the server has size and concurrency protections but no notion of requests-per-interval, and no per-user accounting to attach such limits to.

Other schedules in those tests include `*/5 * * * *`, `0 9 * * *`, `0 */2 * * *`, and `0 1 * * 0`, all similarly illustrative.

Database cleanup in this codebase is event-driven instead of scheduled: cascading deletes happen inline when a user or memo is removed, for example the transactional multi-table delete in `store/db/sqlite/user_delete.go` and the memo relation/attachment cleanup noted at `server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go:579`. **Schema definitions** live in `proto/api/v1/`: `memo_service.proto`, `user_service.proto`, `auth_service.proto`, `attachment_service.proto`, `ai_service.proto`, `idp_service.proto`, `instance_service.proto`, `shortcut_service.proto`, and `common.proto`. REST via grpc-gateway — eight service handlers registered on a `runtime.NewServeMux` (lines 99-122), mounted at `/api/v1/*` and `/file/*` (lines 128-129).

Connect RPC for browser clients, explicitly replacing grpc-web, mounted at `/memos.api.v1.*` (lines 139-144) with metadata, logging, recovery, and auth interceptors.

Server-Sent Events for live updates, registered alongside the gateway group at line 125 so it shares the same CORS treatment.

Outside that package there are three more non-gRPC HTTP surfaces: the file server routes for attachments and avatars (`server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go:121-125`), RSS feeds (`server/router/rss/rss.go`), and an MCP endpoint (`server/router/mcp/`), all wired in `server/server.go:81-96`.

**Machine-readable spec:** an OpenAPI 3 document generated from the protos at `proto/gen/openapi.yaml`, embedded into the binary via `go:embed` in `proto/openapi_embed.go`. That is the closest analogue to the schema artifact the question was after — a REST/OpenAPI contract rather than a GraphQL SDL.
